name: Hoover
label: Dischord
lede: A guitarist who kept playing along at rehearsals turned Victor Deluxe into Hoover: three singers, one nearly hour-long album, and a split once the tour ended.

eras.title: Everybody moved here
eras.text: In the early '90s D.C.'s underground was booming and pulling people in from all over. Dischord says Ian MacKaye had met most of Hoover's future members in their hometowns while touring with Fugazi, then kept running into them once they landed in D.C.

years.h: A Harrisburg guitarist and a D.C. drummer start Victor Deluxe
years.p: [[Joe McRedmond|132df41f-6981-4db5-93cc-47aa88b825c9]], from Harrisburg's Admiral, and Christopher Farrall, from D.C.'s Fine Day, start a band called Victor Deluxe. The original bassist is Geoff Farina.

years.h: [[Fred Erskine|4e2f1c33-e9a9-4aff-9b90-d9b1d3e8af19]] takes over bass, and brings a trumpet
years.p: Erskine, from Nebraska, replaces Geoff Farina, who has left for New England. He started on violin at four and trumpet at eight.
years.xp: DCist's account has Farina leaving for New England and Erskine, a Nebraska native, stepping in on bass. The trumpet stays in the band: Wikipedia lists Erskine on bass, vocals and trumpet.

years.big: He'd listen and get jealous that he wasn't in a band
years.h: Alex Dunham plays along until they ask him to join
years.p: Alex Dunham, newly arrived from Arizona hardcore band Winds of Change, keeps turning up at Victor Deluxe practices. McRedmond tells DCist how that went. Once he's in, there are three singers and the band is Hoover.
years.xp: DCist has McRedmond saying Dunham would start playing his guitar by himself really loud during practices. After a few of those sessions, Farrall suggested asking him in. McRedmond recalls Dunham's answer as "Why didn't you say it a couple weeks ago?"

years.h: Live at Decibels, Mechanicsburg PA, December 20, 1992
yt: Live at Decibels, Mechanicsburg PA, December 20, 1992

eras.title: Three voices, half a label
eras.text: The first single came out as what Dischord calls a Dischord/Hoover Limited half-label release. The sound was already its own: Slint's skeleton, Fugazi's muscle, three members trading whispers and screams.

yt: Live at Decibels, Mechanicsburg, PA, Dec. 1992
years.p: Hoover's first single, cut at Inner Ear. Dischord files it as a Dischord/Hoover Limited half-label release.

years.h: Hoover and Lincoln split a record on Art Monk Construction
years.p: Hoover's Two-Headed Coin shares a record with fellow travelers Lincoln.
Three songs, Return, Private and Dries, that close out the CD reissue of The Lurid Traversal of Route 7 years later.

eras.title: Route 7, then the exit
eras.text: The album arrived in early 1994 and the band was done by spring. AllMusic's Charles Spano argues that late-'90s Fugazi may owe Hoover a debt, not the other way around.

years.p: Recorded at WGNS in August 1993 with [[Geoff Turner|591fc466-2668-4524-852d-a6cc5f18cff7]] and Juan Carrera producing: ten songs, nearly an hour. AllMusic says Hoover was wrongly dubbed a Fugazi copycat.
years.xp:
Electrolux and Cuts Like Drugs each run past seven minutes. Wikipedia calls the band more experimental and permissive than Fugazi, with jazz and dub in the mix, and three of the four members sharing vocals equally.

AllMusic's Ned Raggett heard Drive Like Jehu in it: aggression amped up, lyrics clipped, vocals screamed. The A.V. Club's Jason Heller later called it one of the decade's singular, eerie post-hardcore albums.

Spano's AllMusic biography adds the loud-soft dynamic Slint explored and Mogwai later perfected.

years.h: Back from tour in April, Hoover announce the split
years.p: Hoover tours behind the album, gets back to D.C. and calls it. Dischord dates the band from summer 1992 to spring 1994: under two years.

eras.title: Everyone scatters, the record grows
eras.text: Hoover's members fanned out into new bands in D.C. and Louisville, and the album kept finding people. Every so often Hoover came back to finish something.

years.h: After the split, everyone starts something else
years.p: Joe McRedmond and Fred Erskine form [[The Crownhate Ruin|6c13db70-bd59-44a0-8c6a-eeb0d0c8f40d]]; Erskine then joins Louisville's [[June of 44|56f3de75-2c88-4054-a1df-65c661f4ee0f]]. Alex Dunham starts [[Regulator Watts|5f06481f-d8e3-45b6-954d-753abe05952b]] and later Abilene.
years.xp: The Crownhate Ruin ended after 1995's Until the Eagle Grins. DCist calls Hoover "ground zero" for what followed: ex-members also turned up in HiM and [[Beauty Pill|976b28a1-dd68-4c43-ba08-ba15b58963b2]].

years.h: Four leftover songs come out on Slowdime in 1998
years.p: Hoover regroups briefly in 1997 to record the four songs written before the 1994 split. The self-titled record is distributed by Dischord.

years.h: Ten years after the split, Hoover play again
years.p: Hoover reunites for shows in the US and Europe, per Wikipedia. One of them is Glasgow, December 10, 2004.

years.h: The Lurid Traversal of Route 7 returns on CD, with extras
years.p: Dischord reissues the album with the three Private 7" songs added, running it to thirteen tracks.

years.h: A seven-minute song lands at No. 86 on Vulture's emo list
years.p: Vulture ranks Electrolux, from The Lurid Traversal of Route 7, No. 86 on its 100 greatest emo songs.
